L2-S2.explanation: A contusion is a bruise without a break in the skin or mucosa, with subcutaneous or submucosal haemorrhage.

L11-S2.explanation: A contusion is a bruise without a break in the skin or mucosa, with subcutaneous or submucosal haemorrhage.

L2-S3.explanation: Vital pulp therapy (partial pulpotomy) and pulp space revascularisation/regenerative endodontics allow continued root development; MTA apexification, first-stage endodontics and gutta-percha obturation do not.
L2-S3.source: Course L8-S5, L8-S6 ('Continued root development is expected in teeth with open apices'), L9-S17, L9-S34 ('MTA apexification ... will prevent any further root development'); IADT 2020 Fractures & Luxations (Bourguignon et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:314-330), Table 4
L2-S3.reviewer_note: The AAE glossary definition quoted on L3-S3 defines Apexification as 'a method to induce a calcified barrier ... or the continued apical development of an incompletely formed root in teeth with necrotic pulps'. Read literally, this would make 'Apexification' also correct, contradicting L9-S34. Please confirm Apexification is NOT a correct option (and consider adjusting L3-S3 or the option wording).

L11-S3.explanation: Vital pulp therapy (partial pulpotomy) and pulp space revascularisation/regenerative endodontics allow continued root development; MTA apexification, first-stage endodontics and gutta-percha obturation do not.
L11-S3.source: Course L8-S5, L8-S6 ('Continued root development is expected in teeth with open apices'), L9-S17, L9-S34 ('MTA apexification ... will prevent any further root development'); IADT 2020 Fractures & Luxations (Bourguignon et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:314-330), Table 4
L11-S3.reviewer_note: The AAE glossary definition quoted on L3-S3 defines Apexification as 'a method to induce a calcified barrier ... or the continued apical development of an incompletely formed root in teeth with necrotic pulps'. Read literally, this would make 'Apexification' also correct, contradicting L9-S34. Please confirm Apexification is NOT a correct option (and consider adjusting L3-S3 or the option wording).

L2-S4.explanation: Treatment aims to protect the pulp and restore function and aesthetics: tooth fragment reattachment, composite resin restoration or a temporary glass ionomer restoration.
L2-S4.source: Course L7-S8 (Treatment); IADT 2020 Fractures & Luxations (Bourguignon et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:314-330), Table 2 (enamel-dentin fracture)
L2-S4.reviewer_note: Calcium hydroxide lining (if dentine within 0.5 mm of the pulp) is also part of IADT Table 2 but is not offered as an option. Fluoride varnish is not mentioned in the course or IADT.

L11-S4.explanation: Treatment aims to protect the pulp and restore function and aesthetics: tooth fragment reattachment, composite resin restoration or a temporary glass ionomer restoration.
L11-S4.source: Course L7-S8 (Treatment); IADT 2020 Fractures & Luxations (Bourguignon et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:314-330), Table 2 (enamel-dentin fracture)
L11-S4.reviewer_note: Calcium hydroxide lining (if dentine within 0.5 mm of the pulp) is also part of IADT Table 2 but is not offered as an option. Fluoride varnish is not mentioned in the course or IADT.

L2-S5.explanation: Replacement resorption (ankylosis) cannot be arrested or repaired.

L11-S5.explanation: Replacement resorption (ankylosis) cannot be arrested or repaired.

L2-S6.explanation: The combination of bacteria in the root canal (pulp necrosis) AND cemental/PDL damage on the external root surface results in external inflammatory root resorption.

L11-S6.explanation: The combination of bacteria in the root canal (pulp necrosis) AND cemental/PDL damage on the external root surface results in external inflammatory root resorption.

L2-S7.explanation: Replanted permanent teeth should be stabilised for 2 weeks with a passive, flexible splint (4 weeks only if there is an associated alveolar or jaw-bone fracture).
L2-S7.source: Course L6-S4, L9-S9, L9-S26; IADT 2020 Avulsion of Permanent Teeth (Fouad et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:331-342), section 8 (Stabilization of replanted teeth)

L11-S7.explanation: Replanted permanent teeth should be stabilised for 2 weeks with a passive, flexible splint (4 weeks only if there is an associated alveolar or jaw-bone fracture).
L11-S7.source: Course L6-S4, L9-S9, L9-S26; IADT 2020 Avulsion of Permanent Teeth (Fouad et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:331-342), section 8 (Stabilization of replanted teeth)

L2-S8.explanation: Apexification is a method to induce a calcified barrier in a root with an open apex in teeth with necrotic pulps.

L11-S8.explanation: Apexification is a method to induce a calcified barrier in a root with an open apex in teeth with necrotic pulps.

L2-S9.explanation: Replacement resorption (ankylosis) presents with reduced mobility and a high (metallic) percussion tone; it is the expected outcome after long extra-oral time (>60 min).
L2-S9.source: Course L3-S15, L5-S6, L9-S16; IADT 2020 Avulsion of Permanent Teeth (Fouad et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:331-342), section 11.3

L11-S9.explanation: Replacement resorption (ankylosis) presents with reduced mobility and a high (metallic) percussion tone; it is the expected outcome after long extra-oral time (>60 min).

L2-S10.explanation: The fracture extends below the gingival margin palatally (crown-root fracture) and the pulp is exposed, so this is a complicated crown-root fracture.
L2-S10.source: Course L3-S9 (Crown-root fracture); IADT 2020 Fractures & Luxations (Bourguignon et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:314-330), Table 6
L2-S10.reviewer_note: Image-dependent. Proposed from the image (fracture line running subgingivally on the palatal aspect with a dark area consistent with pulp exposure in the close-up). Please confirm pulp exposure; if the dark area is not the pulp, the answer would be 'Uncomplicated crown-root fracture'.

L2-S11.explanation: IADT recommends splinting for luxated, avulsed and root-fractured teeth; crown fractures without an associated luxation do not need a splint.
L2-S11.source: Course L6-S3, L6-S4; IADT 2020 Fractures & Luxations (Bourguignon et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:314-330), section 6 and Tables 2, 4, 9
L2-S11.reviewer_note: Subluxation is ambiguous: IADT Table 9 says 'Normally no treatment is needed; a passive and flexible splint ... for up to 2 wk may be used but only if there is excessive mobility or tenderness'. The course (L6-S3) says splinting 'might be also recommended' for subluxation, so it is proposed as NOT part of the answer. Please decide whether 'Subluxation' should also be ticked, or reword the question (e.g. 'routinely recommended').

L2-S12.explanation: This is an enamel-dentine-pulp (complicated crown) fracture in an immature tooth seen early; partial (Cvek) pulpotomy preserves the pulp and promotes further root development.
L2-S12.source: Course L8-S3, L8-S5; IADT 2020 Fractures & Luxations (Bourguignon et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:314-330), Table 4
L2-S12.reviewer_note: Same photograph as L3-S24 (identified there as enamel-dentine-pulp fracture). The exposure looks small; IADT Table 4 also allows pulp capping, but direct pulp capping is not an option here, so no conflict.

L2-S13.source: Course L5-S11; IADT 2020 Fractures & Luxations (Bourguignon et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:314-330), section 5.1 (Sensibility tests)

L2-S19.explanation: 11: no crown or root fracture, lateral luxation, immature apex, alveolar fracture [(11) 00Li+]; 21: enamel-dentine fracture, immature apex, no luxation [(21) 20Ni-]; intra-oral (gingival) laceration = 6.
L2-S19.reviewer_note: Reasoning: FDI notation excludes '[(8) ... (9) ...]'. Tooth 11 is displaced with gingival bleeding -> 00L (lateral luxation), i (immature), + (alveolar fracture, as in all three L-options). Tooth 21 has a small mesio-incisal enamel-dentine fracture without visible pulp exposure -> 20Ni-. Apices of both teeth are immature (young mixed dentition, laterals not erupted), so options giving 21 a mature apex (m) are inconsistent. Soft tissue: the gingival laceration around 11 is intra-oral -> superscript 6 (2 would be skin/lip laceration, not visible). Points to check: (a) presence of an alveolar fracture (+) cannot be confirmed from the image; (b) whether 11 is lateral or extrusive luxation; (c) the slide is multi-select ('You can select more than one answer') but only one option is correct - consider making it single-choice.

L3-S25.explanation: Necrotic pulp (negative sensibility tests) plus PDL damage after avulsion, with radiolucent areas along the root a month after replantation, indicates external inflammatory root resorption.

L3-S26.explanation: The tooth is in infra-occlusion relative to the adjacent teeth and the root is being replaced by bone, the signs of replacement resorption (ankylosis) in a growing child.

L3-S27.explanation: Root fracture: involves dentine, cementum and the pulp. Intrusive luxation: displacement of the tooth into the alveolar bone. Subluxation: injury to the supporting structures with abnormal loosening but no displacement. Enamel-dentine fracture: loss of enamel and dentine without pulp involvement.
L3-S27.source: Course L3-S9, L3-S11; IADT 2020 Fractures & Luxations (Bourguignon et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:314-330), Tables 2, 7, 9, 13
L3-S27.reviewer_note: The slide title 'Match the products with their attributes' looks like a leftover platform template; suggest 'Match each injury with its definition'.

L5-S29.explanation: False - a temporary loss of sensibility is a frequent finding during post-traumatic pulp healing and is not conclusive for pulp necrosis; endodontic treatment should not be started solely on the basis of no response to sensibility testing.
L5-S29.source: Course L5-S11; IADT 2020 Fractures & Luxations (Bourguignon et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:314-330), section 5.1 and Table 11 (extrusive luxation, favourable outcomes)
explanations: False - a temporary loss of sensibility is a frequent finding during post-traumatic pulp healing and is not conclusive for pulp necrosis; endodontic treatment should not be started solely on the basis of no response to sensibility testing.

L6-S7.explanation: Avulsion: 2 weeks. Subluxation: a splint for up to 2 weeks only if there is excessive mobility or tenderness on biting. Root fracture: 4 weeks, up to 4 months if the fracture is cervical.
L6-S7.source: Course L6-S4; IADT 2020 Fractures & Luxations (Bourguignon et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:314-330), Tables 7 and 9; IADT 2020 Avulsion of Permanent Teeth (Fouad et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:331-342), section 8
L6-S7.reviewer_note: STRUCTURE PROBLEM: this is a grouped question (one choice per injury) with the options listed inside items, on the website it is shown as one drop-down choice per injury. Proposed answers per group (index within each group's list): Avulsion -> '2 weeks' (0); Subluxation -> '2 weeks if increased mobility' (2); Root fracture -> '4 weeks to 4 months' (0). Recommend splitting into three single-choice slides (or a matching item) so it can be keyed. Note 'Root fracture: 4 weeks to 4 months' simplifies the guideline (4 weeks; up to 4 months for cervical fractures).

L6-S8.explanation: Extrusive luxation: stabilise the tooth for 2 weeks using a passive and flexible splint.
L6-S8.source: Course L6-S4; IADT 2020 Fractures & Luxations (Bourguignon et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:314-330), Table 11 (extrusive luxation)
L6-S8.reviewer_note: Image-dependent and the image is cut off at the bottom. The upper left central incisor appears elongated/displaced incisally (extrusion) -> 2 weeks. L6-S9.explanation: When surgical repositioning of an intruded tooth is indicated, the tooth should be splinted with a passive and flexible splint for 4 weeks.
L6-S9.source: Course L6-S5; IADT 2020 Fractures & Luxations (Bourguignon et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:314-330), Table 13 (intrusive luxation)
L6-S9.reviewer_note: Typo in the stem: 'respositioned'. Option '4 weeks up to 4 months.' has a trailing full stop.

L6-S10.explanation: The splint should include at least one uninjured tooth on either side of the injured tooth: 11-21-22.

L7-S14.explanation: See the explanation given for each statement.
L7-S14.source: Course L7-S5, L7-S8, L7-S9, L7-S10, L7-S16; IADT 2020 Fractures & Luxations (Bourguignon et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:314-330), Tables 2 and 3
L7-S14.reviewer_note: No author key captured (swipe directions not visible). Statement 3 contains 'always ... in cases if fragment unaccounted for AND there are soft tissue injuries' (true, matches IADT), while statement 5 says 'always ... to locate the missing fragment' with no soft-tissue condition (proposed false) - the difference is subtle; please confirm this is intended. Statement 6 is a modified copy of the IADT wording ('within 0.5 mm of the pulp (pink but no bleeding)') where the correct treatment is a calcium hydroxide lining, so it is proposed false. Statement 8 ('non-restorative treatment') is proposed true based on the authors' own L7-S16 feedback ('no treatment, polish sharp edges'). Statement 3 wording 'in cases if' and statement 6 trailing comma.
explanations: False - the exposed dentine should be covered at the emergency visit (fragment reattachment, composite or temporary glass ionomer); revascularisation is not relevant to an enamel-dentine fracture.
False - clinical and radiographic evaluations are needed after 6-8 weeks and after 1 year.
True - if the fragment is missing and there are soft tissue injuries, radiographs of the lip and/or cheek are indicated to search for tooth fragments and/or foreign materials.
True - treatment consists primarily of protecting the pulp from external insults, e.g. covering the dentine to prevent bacterial invasion into the dentinal tubules.
False - a soft tissue radiograph is indicated only when the fragment is missing AND there are soft tissue injuries.

False - if the exposed dentine is within 0.5 mm of the pulp (pink but no bleeding), a calcium hydroxide lining is placed and covered (e.g. with glass ionomer); partial pulpotomy is for pulp exposures.
True - if there is an associated luxation, root fracture or suspicion of an associated luxation injury, the luxation follow-up regimen prevails.
True - minor enamel fractures can be managed without a restoration (no treatment or smoothing/polishing of sharp edges).

L7-S15.explanation:
According to the IADT 2020 guidelines, clinical and radiographic evaluations are necessary:
- After 6-8 weeks
- After 1 year
L7-S15.source: Course L7-S8 (Follow-up); IADT 2020 Fractures & Luxations (Bourguignon et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:314-330), Table 2
L7-S15.reviewer_note: CONTRADICTION in the original: the learner selected this option and the app showed 'Not quite...', yet the authors' feedback text supports this option (6-8 weeks and 1 year) and the other two options are clearly wrong. Either the original key was mis-set or the option was considered incomplete because it omits the 1-year review. Suggest rewording the option to 'Yes. The patient should return after 6-8 weeks and after 1 year for clinical and radiographic examination.'

L7-S16.explanation: Treatment options for enamel fractures (no dentine exposure) include no treatment, polish sharp edges or composite resin restoration.
L7-S16.source: Original author feedback; course L7-S5, L7-S6; IADT 2020 Fractures & Luxations (Bourguignon et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:314-330), Table 3 (enamel-only fracture)
L7-S16.reviewer_note: The authors' feedback names all three options. Note the course page L7-S5 lists 'Polishing of tooth edges, Tooth fragment reattachment, Composite resin restoration' and does not mention 'no treatment' - consider adding it there for consistency.

L8-S9.explanation: Complicated crown fractures: clinical and radiographic evaluations after 6-8 weeks, 3 months, 6 months and 1 year (12 months).
L8-S9.source: Course L8-S3 (Follow-up); IADT 2020 Fractures & Luxations (Bourguignon et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:314-330), Table 4
L8-S9.reviewer_note: The guideline says '1 y'; the blank asks for months, so the last blank is proposed as '12'. The website compares text exactly, so a learner typing '1' (year) will be marked wrong - consider rewording to '... after _, _ months and _ year' or accepting both. The displayed blank lengths ('__', '_', '___') do not correspond to the answers' lengths.

L8-S11.explanation: Partial (Cvek) pulpotomy has a high success rate in teeth with open apices but can also be used in teeth with closed apices.
L8-S11.source: Course L8-S3, L8-S5; IADT 2020 Fractures & Luxations (Bourguignon et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:314-330), Table 4

L9-S18.explanation: See the explanation given for each statement.
L9-S18.source: Course L5-S3, L9-S5; IADT 2020 Avulsion of Permanent Teeth (Fouad et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:331-342), section 2 (First aid at the place of accident)
L9-S18.reviewer_note: No author key captured. Statement 2 ('dizzy and disoriented -> hospital') is proposed TRUE on the basis of course L5-S3 (signs of brain injury require hospital referral); the avulsion guideline itself does not address this. Statement 4 ('plastic bag'): IADT 2020 does not list a plastic bag as a storage medium; proposed FALSE because the tooth should go into milk/HBSS/saliva/saline. Statement 5 is proposed FALSE because IADT encourages immediate replantation at the emergency site.
explanations: False - a tooth wrapped in a tissue dries out. If it cannot be replanted, place it as soon as possible in a storage medium (milk, HBSS, saliva or saline).
True - dizziness or disorientation may indicate a head injury; the child needs medical (hospital) assessment first.
False - avoid touching the root. If the tooth is dirty, rinse it gently in milk, saline or the patient's saliva.
False - pick the tooth up by the crown, but place it in a storage medium (milk, HBSS, saliva or saline) rather than a dry plastic bag.
False - immediate replantation at the place of the accident is the best treatment; the parent should be encouraged to replant the tooth.
True - if the tooth is dirty, rinse it gently in milk, saline or the patient's saliva and replant it.

L9-S19.explanation: In descending order of preference, milk, HBSS, saliva (after spitting into a glass for instance), or saline are suitable and convenient storage mediums. Although water is a poor medium, it is better than leaving the tooth to air-dry.
L9-S19.source: Original author feedback; course L9-S5; IADT 2020 Avulsion of Permanent Teeth (Fouad et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:331-342), section 2, point 6
L9-S19.reviewer_note: The question asks for the 'suitable and convenient' media, so 'Water' and 'Dry' are excluded from the key. If the authors want water ranked as 5th (better than dry), the key would be Milk > HBSS > Saliva > Saline > Water.

L9-S20.explanation: The tooth has been replanted immediately or within a very short time (about 15 minutes) at the place of accident.
L9-S20.source: Original author feedback (dial showed 15); course L9-S7; IADT 2020 Avulsion of Permanent Teeth (Fouad et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:331-342), section 3
L9-S20.reviewer_note: Exact-value scoring: a learner entering e.g. 14 or 16 is marked wrong; the guideline says 'about 15 minutes'.

L9-S21.explanation: The PDL cells may be viable but compromised. The tooth has been kept in a storage medium (eg, milk, HBSS (Save-a-Tooth or similar product), saliva, or saline, and the total extra-oral dry time has been <60 minutes).
L9-S21.source: Original author feedback; course L9-S7; IADT 2020 Avulsion of Permanent Teeth (Fouad et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:331-342), section 3
L9-S21.reviewer_note: The learner's dial value was hidden behind the feedback, so the expected value is inferred from the feedback text ('<60 minutes').

L9-S22.explanation: The PDL cells are likely to be non-viable. The total extra-oral dry time has been more than 60 minutes, regardless of the tooth having been stored in a medium or not.
L9-S22.source: Original author feedback; course L9-S7; IADT 2020 Avulsion of Permanent Teeth (Fouad et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:331-342), section 3
L9-S22.reviewer_note: Expected value inferred from the feedback text ('more than 60 minutes'); the learner's ~92 was marked 'Not quite'.

L9-S24.explanation: In avulsed teeth with a closed apex the pulp should be removed and root canal treatment initiated within 2 weeks after replantation; in open-apex teeth root canal treatment is avoided unless pulp necrosis is diagnosed, because revascularisation may occur.
L9-S24.source: Course L9-S9, L9-S10, L9-S13, L9-S17, L9-S31; IADT 2020 Avulsion of Permanent Teeth (Fouad et al., Dent Traumatol 2020;36:331-342), section 10 (Endodontic considerations)
L9-S24.reviewer_note: Author feedback only confirms that option 4 is wrong. Option 3 ('When extraoral dry time is <60min, RCT should not be started unless there are signs of pulp necrosis') is true for open-apex teeth but false for closed-apex teeth; it is proposed as incorrect because it does not specify open apex. Please confirm.
